# Dissecting OGT’s TPR domain to identify determinants of cellular function

**Authors:** Sarah C. Potter; Bettine E. Gibbs; Forrest A. Hammel; Cassandra M. Joiner; Joao A. Paulo; John Janetzko; Zebulon G. Levine; George Q. Fei; Stephen J. Haggarty; Suzanne Walker

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Microbiology, Blavatnik Institute of Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115 | bChemical Neurobiology Laboratory, Center for Genomic Medicine, Department of Neurology, Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02114 | cDepartment of Cell Biology, Blavatnik Institute of Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115 | dDepartment of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138

## Abstract

OGT is the sole glycosyltransferase operating in the nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments of mammalian cells. OGT is essential in animals, but elucidating functions important for cell viability has been challenging because OGT modifies thousands of proteins and has numerous stable binding partners. One way to assess OGT’s most important functions is to identify molecular determinants required to support viability and then to characterize how viable variants differ from wild-type OGT and nonviable variants. Here, we investigate how OGT’s TPR domain impacts growth and other cellular phenotypes. The shortest TPR truncation that sustains cell viability has lost several functions characteristic of wild-type OGT, making it potentially useful for identifying the functions that are essential for cell growth.

## Abstract

O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) is an essential mammalian enzyme that glycosylates myriad intracellular proteins and cleaves the transcriptional coregulator Host Cell Factor 1 to regulate cell cycle processes. Via these catalytic activities as well as noncatalytic protein–protein interactions, OGT maintains cell homeostasis. OGT’s tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domain is important in substrate recognition, but there is little information on how changing the TPR domain impacts its cellular functions. Here, we investigate how altering OGT’s TPR domain impacts cell growth after the endogenous enzyme is deleted. We find that disrupting the TPR residues required for OGT dimerization leads to faster cell growth, whereas truncating the TPR domain slows cell growth. We also find that OGT requires eight of its 13 TPRs to sustain cell viability. OGT-8, like the nonviable shorter OGT variants, is mislocalized and has reduced Ser/Thr glycosylation activity; moreover, its interactions with most of wild-type OGT’s binding partners are broadly attenuated. Therefore, although OGT’s five N-terminal TPRs are not essential for cell viability, they are required for proper subcellular localization and for mediating many of OGT’s protein–protein interactions. Because the viable OGT truncation variant we have identified preserves OGT’s essential functions, it may facilitate their identification.

O-linked N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) transferase (OGT) is an evolutionarily conserved metazoan enzyme that has been linked to a wide array of cellular processes, including transcription, translation, protein homeostasis, metabolism, and cellular stress response (1–9). OGT influences these processes by catalyzing the posttranslational modification known as O-GlcNAcylation, by cleaving the essential transcriptional coregulator Host Cell Factor 1 (HCF-1), and by binding other proteins (Fig. 1 A–C) (9–12). OGT is unique in being the only glycosyltransferase found in the nucleus and the cytoplasm rather than the secretory pathway (13–15), and it is notably promiscuous. For example, in T cells, OGT glycosylates over 1,000 different proteins, some at more than one site (16). Because it has so many substrates and binding partners, and may play distinct roles in different cell types, deconvoluting OGT’s biological functions is a challenge.

(B) OGT cleaves HCF-1 via addition of O-GlcNAc on key glutamate residues. (C) OGT forms multiple protein complexes. (D) A composite crystal structure illustrates OGT’s catalytic domain (gray) and TPR domain (pink) bound to UDP (blue) and an HCF-1-derived peptide (yellow); PDB: 1W3B adapted from ref. 17 and 4N3B adapted from ref. 11.*

OGT is required for mammalian cell proliferation, and one of our goals is to identify its essential functions (10). To address this question, we previously developed an approach to replace endogenous Ogt in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) with variants lacking specified biochemical functions (9). Using this system, we found that OGT’s ability to effect O-GlcNAcylation is required for viability, but its ability to cleave HCF-1 is not. We also found that when wild-type (WT) OGT is depleted to such low levels that O-GlcNAcylation is undetectable by immunoblot analysis, cells remain viable but proliferate extremely slowly. Under these conditions, an ectopic copy of a catalytically dead OGT variant promotes cell growth, implying that noncatalytic functions of OGT are important in cell proliferation. These studies implicated both catalytic and noncatalytic functions of OGT in cell growth but were not designed to identify specific substrates or binding partners as effectors required for proliferation. To find such effectors, it is necessary first to define the minimal OGT variant that supports cell proliferation.

OGT consists of an N-terminal domain comprising 13 tetratricopeptide repeats (TPRs) and a C-terminal catalytic domain (Figs. 1D and 2A) (17–20). TPRs are commonly involved in protein–protein interactions, and OGT’s TPR domain is known to interact with numerous binding partners. It also plays a direct role in substrate selection (21). OGT’s 13 TPRs form an elongated superhelix with a hydrophobic lumen lined with conserved asparagine and aspartate “ladders” (17, 20–25). Unstructured regions of protein substrates and interaction partners bind within OGT’s TPR lumen where they are anchored by bidentate contacts from asparagine ladder residues to the peptide backbone (21, 22, 24). The aspartate ladder residues and other residues that contact substrate side chains provide some degree of substrate and glycosite selectivity (24, 25).

(B) TPR truncation variants show decreased global glycosylation in vitro in HeLa cell extracts. * denotes low level of endogenous OGT in extracts. (C) Ectopic expression of OGT complements the loss of the endogenous Ogt gene; replacement with OGT variants can test which OGT features are required for cell survival. (D) Ectopic OGT variants are expressed at different levels in iCre MEFs. Except for OGT-4 and OGT-5, which are expressed at levels comparable to endogenous OGT, all variants are expressed below the level of endogenous OGT. OGT-4 and OGT-5 appear at the same molecular weight as endogenous OGT so the α-FLAG blot was also included. (E) Live-cell imaging demonstrates rescue of growth by OGT truncation containing 8 complete TPRs. (F) CellTiter-Glo assay supports live-cell imaging results confirming the ability of OGT-8 to sustain cellular viability.*

Here, we sought to define the minimal TPR length required for mammalian cell viability. Truncated OGT variants have been previously studied in cells but only in a background containing full-length endogenous OGT (26). Using MEFs in which endogenous Ogt can be inducibly deleted (27, 28), we engineered cell lines to evaluate a series of TPR-truncated OGT variants for their ability to support growth (9). The shortest TPR truncation variant that can sustain cell viability contains only eight of the 13 full TPRs. Although this truncated variant preserves the functions required for viability in cell culture, it is defective in many respects. Our work therefore highlights the crucial role of OGT’s five N-terminal TPRs in regulating numerous functions, including proper nuclear localization. We also report here that monomeric OGT rescues growth of cells lacking the wild-type enzyme. OGT is known to form dimers and was proposed to function as an obligate dimer, but this study shows that dimerization is not required for growth.

## Results

### OGT Variants with Truncated TPR Domains Show Reduced Glycosylation Activity in HeLa Cell Extracts.

We previously reported a set of OGT TPR truncations containing four to eight full TPRs and characterized their ability to glycosylate three purified substrates (25). Each substrate showed a different glycosylation profile against the set of TPR variants, leading us to conclude that each of these substrates depends on different contacts to the TPR lumen. Because three substrates cannot begin to capture the variety of OGT’s substrate interactions, we have used HeLa cell extracts to assess the glycosylation activity of our OGT truncation variants more broadly. Cell extracts are metabolically active and maintain cellular complexes (29), but unlike with experiments in cells, it is possible to control the concentration of each OGT variant that is added. We incubated purified OGT-WT or a truncated OGT variant (Fig. 2A) with cell extracts and then immunoblotted for O-GlcNAc modifications. All the truncated variants showed reduced glycosylation compared with OGT-WT, with glycosylation decreasing as a function of TPR length (Fig. 2B).

### OGT Containing Eight Full TPRs Rescues Growth after Endogenous Ogt Knockout.

We next sought to determine whether any of the TPR truncation variants could sustain viability in cells given their attenuated glycosylation profiles in cell extracts. To test this, we made use of an Ogt floxed MEF cell line in which endogenous OGT can be inducibly deleted by adding tamoxifen (iCre (inducible Cre-recombinase) MEFs) (Fig. 2C) (27, 28). Ogt deletion results in cell death within a few days, but lentiviral introduction of ectopic wild-type OGT can rescue growth (SI Appendix, Fig. S1) (9). Thus, an OGT variant introduced into iCre MEFs must perform OGT’s essential functions in order for the cells to survive after deletion of endogenous Ogt.

We engineered iCre MEFs to express mKate2-2×FLAG fusions of OGT-WT and the TPR-truncated OGT variants (Fig. 2A) and confirmed expression of each variant via immunoblot (Fig. 2D). Despite sorting for mKate2-positive cells, we observed substantial variation in expression levels of the OGT constructs. Resorting the cells to achieve more consistent expression led to only marginal improvement, possibly because selection bias precludes achieving similar expression levels for all variants. The OGT-4 and OGT-5 variants were expressed at levels similar to endogenous OGT but at high levels compared to the other ectopic variants. OGT-6, OGT-7, and OGT-8 were expressed at lower levels than ectopic OGT-WT.

To test the ability of the TPR-truncated OGT variants to sustain viability, we tracked the confluence of iCre MEFs for 10 d after inducing Ogt deletion. Control experiments in which endogenous OGT was still present showed similar growth rates for all cell lines (SI Appendix, Fig. S2), implying that elevated expression of OGT-4 and OGT-5 is not inherently toxic to the cells. Consistent with previous results (9), we found that cells without ectopic OGT stopped proliferating and died a few days after endogenous Ogt knockout, while the addition of ectopic OGT-WT rescued viability. Although ectopic OGT variants having seven or fewer TPRs were unable to rescue growth after inducible Ogt knockout, cells expressing the variant containing eight full TPRs (OGT-8) were viable at 10 d posttreatment (Fig. 2E). As an orthogonal measure of cell viability, we performed CellTiter-Glo assays to measure adenosine triphosphate (ATP) at regular intervals following Ogt deletion (Fig. 2F). ATP levels in cells lacking ectopic OGT or expressing the OGT variants with seven or fewer TPRs plateaued around day three postknockout and decreased to baseline by day 10. In contrast, cells expressing ectopic OGT-8 or OGT-WT were still viable and metabolically active on day 10. These experiments showed that cells expressing an OGT variant that lacks the first five TPRs are viable and can proliferate in a cell culture model, albeit more slowly than cells expressing full-length OGT. OGT-8 must therefore perform the key OGT functions that are essential for supporting cell growth.

### Cellular O-GlcNAc Levels Do Not Determine the Viability Differences of TPR Truncation Variants.

We next examined the O-GlcNAc profiles of cells expressing TPR truncation variants. In vitro, OGT-8 showed higher glycosylation activity than the shorter truncation variants (Fig. 2B). Because O-GlcNAcylation is OGT’s essential catalytic function (9), we wondered whether OGT-8 appeared more active than the shorter truncation variants in cells, thus explaining why OGT-8 can sustain viability in iCre MEFs while the shorter variants cannot. Because there is a multiday delay between Ogt knockout and significant depletion of O-GlcNAc (9), we harvested iCre cells expressing our TPR truncation variants at 2 and 4 d post-Ogt deletion. Untreated cells were harvested on day zero as a control. Immunoblot analysis of O-GlcNAc levels showed reduced O-GlcNAc in all cell lines expressing TPR truncation variants, including OGT-8, compared to cells expressing ectopic OGT-WT (Fig. 3A).

*Fig. 3.: TPR truncation attenuates O-GlcNAcylation in cells. (A) iCre MEFs expressing the panel of OGT-TPR truncations were harvested at day 0, 2, or 4 after endogenous OGT knockout. A pan-O-GlcNAc antibody reveals broadly diminished O-GlcNAc signal for each of the TPR truncation variants compared to ectopic OGT-WT. (B) Schematic showing the generation of iCre-dTAG MEFs and subsequent introduction of an ectopic OGT variant of interest. (C) iCre-dTAG MEFs expressing the panel of OGT-TPR truncations were harvested at day 0, 1, or 2 after initiating FKBP12F36V-OGT-WT degradation. A pan-O-GlcNAc antibody reveals broadly diminished O-GlcNAc signal for each of the TPR truncation variants compared to ectopic OGT-WT.*

An issue with analyzing iCre MEFs 4 d after Ogt deletion is that cells expressing OGT variants that cannot rescue growth are in the process of dying (Fig. 2 E and F). To ensure that observations about OGT variants were not confounded by the processes that lead to cell death, we previously developed an iCre cell line in which the sole copy of OGT bears a conditional degron tag (dTAG) that enables inducible, rapid OGT degradation upon the addition of a small molecule degrader compound (9). Whereas iCre MEFs die upon Ogt deletion, iCre-dTAG MEFs stop proliferating but remain viable due to the presence of very low levels of O-GlcNAc. Nonviable variants can be studied in this background without the confounding effects of ongoing cell death. We engineered iCre-dTAG MEFs to express either a nondegradable copy of OGT-WT or a TPR truncation variant (Fig. 3B). Expression of all the truncation variants promoted proliferation above the background condition of no ectopic OGT (SI Appendix, Fig. S3). After treating the cells with degrader compound for 1 and 2 d, we harvested iCre-dTAG MEFs expressing each of the variants; untreated cells were harvested as a control. Immunoblot analysis of O-GlcNAc levels showed that global O-GlcNAc levels were greatly reduced in the iCre-dTAG MEFs expressing TPR truncation variants compared to those expressing ectopic OGT-WT (Fig. 3C). The attenuated O-GlcNAc levels in cells expressing OGT-8, OGT-7, and OGT-6 compared with OGT-WT reflects both their lower enzymatic activity and their low expression levels. OGT-5 and OGT-4 showed good expression, but the signal due to glycosylation was nevertheless low, consistent with the in vitro results (Fig. 2B). We conclude that global O-GlcNAc levels do not determine viability because these levels are similar in cells expressing the viable OGT-8 variant and cells expressing the shorter nonviable variants.

### Truncated OGT Variants Mislocalize to the Cytoplasm.

We next considered the possibility that viable and nonviable OGT variants might localize differently in cells, accounting at least partially for the viability differences. Wild-type OGT localizes to both the nucleus and cytoplasm but with a higher nuclear signal (17, 30, 31). The TPR domain alone localizes similarly to wild-type OGT (32), suggesting that the TPR domain encodes the information required for nuclear localization. Consistent with this, OGT variants lacking most of the TPR domain mislocalize to the cytoplasm (26).

We investigated the localization of the truncation variants to assess whether cell viability is correlated with wild-type-like localization. We first confirmed that the TPR domain alone was sufficient for nuclear localization in MEFs. As expected, an mKate2-2×FLAG-tagged, TPR-only variant (OGT-TPR) localized to the nucleus and cytoplasm in iCre-dTAG MEFs, with higher relative signal in the nucleus (Fig. 4 A, Left). OGT-WT (Fig. 4B) showed similar localization. Curiously, however, the TPR-only variant did not localize properly in cells when the background copy of wild-type OGT was degraded. Instead, it accumulated in a distinctive outline around the nucleus (Fig. 4 A, Center). To test whether this phenotype was due to loss of full-length OGT or loss of O-GlcNAc, we treated cells with the OGT inhibitor OSMI-4 and again observed perinuclear accumulation of the TPR-only variant (Fig. 4 A, Right). The fluorescently tagged OGT-WT variant did not show perinuclear accumulation upon OGT inhibition (Fig. 4B). We have concluded that proper subcellular localization of the TPR-only variant is dependent on O-GlcNAc and suggest that its accumulation is due to interactions with proteins in the perinuclear region that are normally glycosylated. OGT’s TPR lumen binds unstructured regions of proteins and glycosylation of these unstructured regions would be expected to block binding in the lumen. Because it is not “capped” by the active site, the TPR-only construct may interact with some proteins that the full-length protein cannot.

*Fig. 4.: OGT’s N-terminal TPRs are necessary for nuclear localization. Live-cell confocal fluorescence microscopy was used to determine the subcellular localization of an ectopic mKate2-2×FLAG-tagged TPR-only variant (A) or OGT-WT (B) in iCre-dTAG MEFs. Localization of the TPR-only variant of OGT is dependent on cellular O-GlcNAc. (C) OGT-TPR truncation variants are mislocalized to the cytoplasm. Acquisition and display setting were adjusted for some variants to enable optimal visualization of the localization phenotypes; direct comparison of signal intensity should not be made between micrographs.*

We next characterized the subcellular localization of our panel of TPR truncation variants in iCre-dTAG MEFs. Live-cell confocal microscopy showed that all the TPR truncation variants, including OGT-8, localized primarily to the cytoplasm, with only a faint signal in the nucleus (Fig. 4C). Localization of these TPR truncation variants was unaffected by the presence of the background copy of FKBP12-OGT-WT (SI Appendix, Fig. S4A). These results show that the five N-terminal TPRs of OGT are required for proper localization to the nucleus. A previous report identified an Asp-Phe-Pro (DFP) motif at the C terminus of TPR 13 as a noncanonical nuclear localization signal that is sufficient to direct OGT’s localization to the nuclear compartment (33). Because all the truncation constructs contain this DFP motif, we concluded that it is not sufficient for nuclear localization in MEFs. To test whether it plays any role in nuclear localization, we engineered iCre-dTAG MEFs to express a full-length OGT variant containing three alanines in place of the DFP motif (OGTDFP→AAA). Live-cell confocal microscopy showed that the OGTDFP→AAA variant, just like OGT-WT, localized to the nucleus and the cytoplasm, with a higher relative nuclear signal (SI Appendix, Fig. S5). This finding confirmed what our observation of mislocalization of the TPR-truncated variants of OGT had suggested: OGT’s DFP motif does not act as a nuclear localization signal in MEFs. Whether the N-terminal five TPRs of OGT are sufficient for OGT’s nuclear localization remains to be determined, but this work shows that they are necessary. Because OGT-8 is mislocalized but viable, any essential nuclear functions of OGT-8 are met despite low levels of protein in the nucleus.

### OGT Homodimerization Is Not Essential for Viability.

Another possible explanation for the viability of cells expressing OGT-8 compared to the shorter truncation variants is that OGT-8 contains the interface required for OGT homodimerization whereas the shorter truncation variants do not. Structural studies revealed that OGT forms a dimer, with residues on the convex surface of TPRs 6 and 7 forming the dimer interface (Fig. 5A), and it has been shown for a small number of substrates that disrupting the dimer interface reduces substrate glycosylation (17, 22, 34). It has therefore been suggested that OGT functions as a dimer in cells, but whether OGT’s dimer interface is necessary for cell viability has not been examined. To determine whether OGT’s dimer interface is required for cell growth, we engineered iCre MEFs to express a full-length OGT variant with two amino acid changes that prevent dimerization: W198E and I201D (numbering for the 1,036 amino acid isoform) (17, 22). Growth assays showed that cells expressing the dimer-disrupted OGT variant, OGT-monomer, remained viable after deletion of endogenous Ogt (Fig. 5B). In fact, despite lower expression of OGT-monomer, cells with this construct grew faster than cells expressing ectopic OGT-WT. Immunoblot analysis also revealed that iCre MEFs expressing OGT-monomer as the only copy of OGT retained broad O-GlcNAcylation activity, although the depletion of some bands in the O-GlcNAc immunoblot suggests that dimerization is required for glycosylation of some cellular substrates (Fig. 5C). Given that the homodimerization interface is not essential to sustain viability of full length OGT, it is unlikely that the presence of the homodimer interface in OGT-8 explains its unique ability to sustain cellular viability compared to the shorter truncation variants.

*Fig. 5.: OGT dimerization is not essential for cellular viability. (A) OGT forms a homodimer (Right) mediated primarily by residues in TPR6 (Left). PDB: 1W3B adapted from ref. 17. (B) Live-cell imaging demonstrates that an ectopic OGT variant that cannot dimerize rescues growth after knockout of endogenous Ogt; n = 6 technical replicates per experiment, mean and error bars are from two replicate experiments. (C) iCre MEFs expressing OGT-monomer as the only copy of OGT retain broad O-GlcNAcylation activity; glycosylation of specific substrates appears substantially diminished, denoted by *.*

### TPR Truncation Greatly Alters Protein–Protein Interactions.

Full-length OGT has a large number of binding partners that are involved in a wide array of critical cellular processes (35–39), and many interactors have been shown to interact with OGT’s TPR domain (32, 40–42). We wondered whether the viability of MEFs expressing OGT-8 could be due to OGT-8’s ability to bind many of the same interactors as OGT-WT. Therefore, we performed a pulldown experiment to map the interactomes of OGT-WT, OGT-8, OGT-7, and OGT-4 after treating the relevant iCre-dTAG MEFs with degrader compound for 8 h. iCre-dTAG MEFs with no ectopic OGT were used as our negative control. We immunoprecipitated the OGT variants under native conditions to retain protein–protein interactions and analyzed the elution fraction of each sample via mass spectrometry to identify the interacting proteins (Fig. 6A). Peptides corresponding to ~2,600 different proteins were identified across all five conditions, including the negative control (SI Appendix, S1 File). Hits were classified as proteins that were at least fivefold enriched for an OGT variant averaged across three replicates compared to the negative control, provided that the total peptides for that protein averaged at least two across all three replicates. Across all the cell lines, 113 proteins were classified as hits (Fig. 6B). For OGT-WT, we identified 42 different protein interactors, of which 35 interacted exclusively with OGT-WT and two interacted with all four OGT variants (Fig. 6B). Seventy-four percent of the OGT-WT hits were previously identified as OGT interactors (Fig. 6C) (39). Using a threefold enrichment cutoff, 21 additional proteins were classified as OGT-WT hits, of which nine were previously known wild-type OGT interactors (SI Appendix, S1 File) (39). Based on these results, we concluded that the fivefold enrichment cutoff was sufficiently stringent to include a high percentage of “true” interactors even for the truncations. Seventy-eight of the 113 hit proteins were identified as hits for one or more of the TPR truncation variants, and most of these were not found as hits for OGT-WT either here or in other interactome studies (Fig. 6B) (39).

*Fig. 6.: OGT’s N-terminal TPRs are critical for protein–protein interactions. (A) mKate2-2×FLAG-tagged OGT variants were immunoprecipitated from native cell iCre-dTAG MEF lysates, and subsequent mass spectrometry was performed to identify protein interactors. (B) Intersections of OGT interactor hits are illustrated by an UpSet plot; n = 113 proteins were classified as hits across all four experimental conditions. (C) Most OGT-WT hits do not interact with the OGT truncations. (D) OGT-8 hits illustrate importance of OGT’s N-terminal TPRs for stable interactions with known protein partners. In C and D, known OGT interactors are bolded, and known OGT substrates are italicized; † denotes proteins for which expression data not obtained; * denotes proteins with elevated expression in “hit” cell line.*

We quantified relative protein abundance across cell lines to assess whether differences in the expression of interactors might explain their classification as interactor hits for some OGT variants but not others (SI Appendix, S1 File). With a few exceptions, primarily for proteins classified as OGT- WT or OGT-7 hits, protein abundance was similar across all cell lines. One exception was OGA, which was classified as a hit only in the OGT-WT cell line. OGA expression was higher in this cell line than in any of the other cell lines. Because OGA expression correlates with O-GlcNAc levels (43, 44), which are lower for the truncation variants than for OGT-WT, higher OGA abundance in the OGT-WT cell line is not surprising. However, higher expression may not fully explain the observation that OGA is a hit only for OGT-WT. A recent structure shows that OGA contacts the full TPR domain of OGT (34), and multiple stabilizing contacts would be lost upon TPR domain truncation. Because most interactors are expressed at similar levels across cell lines, we can conclude that differential protein expression does not explain the striking differences in hits between OGT-WT and the shorter OGT variants.

We considered the possibility that loss of interactors upon TPR truncation is due to mislocalization of the TPR truncation variants by analyzing the Cellular Compartment GO terms for each hit (45). Although the percentage of nuclear protein hits decreased upon TPR truncation, all the truncation variants did pull down nuclear proteins (SI Appendix, Fig. S6 and S1 File). For example, 60% of OGT-8 hits localize in some capacity to the nucleus compared with approximately 75% of OGT-WT hits. Therefore, mislocalization of the truncation variants did not preclude them from interacting with nuclear proteins in intact cells and/or postlysis. Taken together, our results suggest that the differences in interacting partners for OGT-WT and the truncation variants are due in large part to the different numbers of TPRs. Because most OGT-WT hits were not found to interact with the OGT truncations (Fig. 6C), the five N-terminal TPRs are necessary for stable interaction with a majority of wild-type OGT’s known protein partners. Whether they are sufficient for interaction is still unknown.

Only two proteins, CPSF1 and TET3, were hits for OGT-WT and OGT-8, but not for either of the nonviable OGT variants (Fig. 6D). Both CPSF1 and TET3 were previously identified as OGT interactors (46, 47) and it is possible that one or both of these proteins contribute to the unique ability of the OGT-8 truncation variant to promote cell viability. CPSF1 is an essential protein involved in pre-mRNA processing that has been implicated in cell cycle regulation (46, 48, 49). TET3 is among a family of well-known OGT interactors that promote DNA demethylation by oxidizing 5-methylcytosine (50). OGT-binding to TET proteins affects their activity and impacts gene expression (47, 51).

HUWE1 and HNRL1 were identified as hits for OGT-8 and at least one shorter OGT variant (Fig. 6D). These proteins are known OGT interactors but did not meet the hit cutoffs for OGT-WT in our experiment. Five other OGT-8 hits deserve comment because all have been previously classified as OGT interactors: PAXB1, P66β, BAG6, UBL4A, and GET4. PAXB1 is a transcriptional regulator that controls muscle cell growth in vitro and in vivo (52, 53). P66β was a weak hit for OGT-8 and barely missed the cutoff for OGT-WT. P66β is a known OGT substrate involved in epigenetic regulation via participation in the nucleosome remodeling and deacetylase complex (54–57). The other three proteins, which form a stable complex, were very strongly enriched in pulldowns with OGT-8 (80-fold for BAG6, 19-fold for UBL4A, and 17-fold for GET4) (Fig. 6D). The BAG6 complex is required for the insertion of tail-anchored proteins into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane (58). To our knowledge, BAG6 is the only member of the BAG6 complex that has been shown to interact directly with OGT (36, 59), so the other members of the complex may be indirect binding partners.

Overall, our results confirm the importance of the TPR domain of OGT in its protein–protein interactions and show that the five N-terminal TPRs are necessary for stabilizing many of these interactions. Consistent with their importance, a residue conservation analysis shows that the five N-terminal TPRs, but not some of the other TPRs, are highly conserved between organisms (SI Appendix, Fig. S7). The N-terminal TPRs have evidently played a critical role in OGT function throughout evolution.

## Discussion

Deconvoluting OGT’s cellular functions has proven challenging despite decades of study. Connections with thousands of substrates and interactors involved in numerous cellular processes have demonstrated the importance of OGT in cellular physiology while making it challenging to identify which functions are required to support cell viability. Here, using our previously developed genetic systems to replace endogenous OGT with variants, we identified the shortest TPR truncation variant that can sustain viability. We showed that cells with an OGT variant possessing eight of the 13 full TPRs can rescue growth after inducible knockout of endogenous Ogt whereas cells with shorter OGT variants die. OGT-8, but not the shorter variants, can therefore perform the OGT functions essential for cellular growth. Further study of this variant compared with others may lead to identification of those essential functions.

By comparing OGT-8 with both OGT-WT and the shorter OGT variants, we found that OGT-8 shares a number of defects with the shorter variants. Notably, all the truncation variants mislocalize to the cytoplasm. It has been reported that OGT variants containing five or fewer TPRs are mislocalized (26), and our work shows that longer OGT variants, including the viable variant with eight TPRs, are also mislocalized. We have therefore concluded that the five N-terminal TPRs of OGT are necessary for nuclear localization in MEFs. The N-terminal TPRs do not contain a canonical nuclear localization sequence and it is still unclear whether these five TPRs are sufficient to transport other proteins into the nucleus. Some proteins enter the nucleus as cargo complexed to other proteins that contain a nuclear localization signal (60). It is therefore possible that OGT is ferried into the nuclear compartment by one or more interacting partners. Because truncating OGT attenuates binding to many partner proteins that localize to the nucleus, our studies provide some support for this model.

We were surprised by the dramatic differences in the proteins classified as interactors for OGT-WT and our panel of truncation variants. Although biochemical studies have shown that the N-terminal TPRs of OGT are important for high-affinity binding of a few protein interactors (40–42), a systematic study of the impact of TPR truncation on OGT’s protein–protein interactions in cells has not, to our knowledge, been conducted previously. We found that most proteins pulled down by wild-type OGT did not interact stably enough with the TPR truncation variants to be classified as hits. Therefore, these interactors either directly contact the N-terminal TPRs or contact other proteins that rely on interactions with the N-terminal TPRs for stable binding.

There is limited structural information on how OGT’s binding partners interact with OGT. The TPR domain of OGT spans ~100 Å, and the lumenal surface contains ladders of asparagines and aspartates (21). Many of OGT’s binding partners and substrates are thought to contain disordered regions that bind in an extended conformation within the TPR lumen (24, 25). One structure of full-length OGT complexed with another protein, OGA, has so far been reported (34). OGA is the glycosidase that removes O-GlcNAc from proteins that have been glycosylated by OGT, and the structure of the OGT-OGA complex shows that OGA’s glycoside hydrolase domain docks to the surface of the C-terminal TPRs while a long, disordered region of OGA extends from OGT’s active site through the entire TPR lumen. Because complexation inhibits activity of both enzymes, it has been proposed that OGT-OGA complex formation can serve as a regulatory mechanism to prevent futile O-GlcNAc cycling (34).

In our pulldown data, OGA was a weak hit for OGT-WT and HCF-1 was the top hit. HCF-1 was also the top hit for OGT-8 and was even detected as a weak hit for OGT-7. HCF-1 is typically one of the most enriched proteins in OGT interactome studies and has been estimated to bind ~50% of cellular OGT (35–38). It must therefore play a major role in regulating OGT biology. HCF-1 contains multiple threonine-rich repeats that bind in OGT’s TPR lumen, and structures of a single HCF-1 repeat bound to a truncated OGT variant have been influential in shaping our understanding of how peptides bind in the TPR lumen (11). These structures show that the conserved OGT asparagine ladder residues make bidentate contacts to every other backbone amide of peptide ligands, while the aspartate residues contact some of the side chains. Results here suggest that other OGT interactors may use threonine-rich regions like those in HCF-1 to bind OGT’s TPR domain. For example, BAG6, a previously identified interactor of OGT, was an extraordinarily strong hit for OGT-8. The OGT-binding region of BAG6 has been localized to a 35 amino acid segment (59) that we note contains a GTTNTATTA motif identical to the threonine-rich TPR binding sequence of HCF-1 (11). Truncating the TPR domain evidently allows BAG6 to compete more effectively for binding to OGT, possibly because other interactors are lost and/or OGT is concentrated in the cytoplasm. A recent study found that under oxidative stress, OGT pulls down less HCF-1 and substantially more BAG6 than under nonstressed conditions, suggesting that redox-responsive regulatory mechanisms shift OGT’s interactome (36). Taken together with our results, these findings suggest that the OGT-BAG6 complex plays a conditionally important cellular role that warrants further investigation. In the meantime, identification of the same TPR binding motif in HCF-1 and BAG6 suggests that it may be possible to use similarity to this threonine-rich motif as a basis for predicting other OGT interactors or substrates that bind in the TPR lumen.

Our efforts to understand the basis of OGT-8’s ability to rescue growth when endogenous Ogt is deleted also led us to examine the importance of OGT homodimerization in viability. It has been speculated that OGT’s ability to dimerize is crucial for its glycosylation activity, and OGT-8 is the only truncation construct with an intact dimer interface. However, we found that disrupting OGT’s dimer interface did not result in reduced growth. Indeed, cells expressing OGT-monomer grew faster than those expressing OGT-WT. Although the dimer interface is not required for cell proliferation, it may play an important role in controlling cell growth. It is currently unknown whether the OGT dimer is the sole form of OGT in cells or whether dimerization is a regulated process.

The work here lays the groundwork for other studies to investigate OGT’s essential functions. We previously showed that O-GlcNAcylation is OGT’s essential catalytic function for cell survival, but we also showed that cells remain viable in culture under conditions of greatly reduced O-GlcNAc (9). OGT-8 displays attenuated glycosylation compared with OGT-WT, but we presume that it retains the ability to glycosylate OGT’s essential substrates and therefore might serve as a tool to uncover them. We also note that a recent study attributed cell death due to OGT deletion to severe mitochondrial dysfunction (8), suggesting that OGT-8 may preserve sufficient mitochondrial function for cells to survive while the shorter variants may not. If so, OGT- 8’s ability to rescue the cytotoxic mitochondrial defects observed in the absence of OGT may help guide future studies to better understand this essential protein.

## Materials and Methods

### Cloning and Molecular Biology.

Plasmids for protein expression and production of lentivirus were generated as previously described (9) and as described in SI Appendix.

### Cell Line Maintenance.

Human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293T (ATCC CRL-3216) cells and all MEF cells were maintained in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) (low glucose with pyruvate, GlutaMAX; ThermoFisher 10567-022) + 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; ThermoFisher 10437-028) + 1× penicillin/streptomycin (Pen/Strep; Corning 30-002-CI) in a 37 °C, 5% CO2 humidified incubator. All cell experiments used cell lines at fewer than 10 passages from receipt or from sorting for newly derived cell lines. Cell lines were regularly checked for mycoplasma using the MycoAlert Detection Kit (Lonza LT07-118). Lentivirus production, transfection, and fluorescent sorting of mKate2-OGT cells are described in SI Appendix.

### OGT Knockout in the Cre/Lox System.

iCre MEF cells were plated 24 h before treatment in DMEM + 10% FBS + 1× Pen/Strep. Medium was changed to DMEM + 10% FBS + 1× Pen/Strep + 1 μM 4-HT (diluted from 10 mM stock in ethanol) at time zero. After 24 h, medium was replaced with DMEM + 10% FBS + 1× Pen/Strep. Medium was changed daily thereafter until cells were collected for lysis.

### OGT Degradation with dTAG-13.

FKBP12F36V-OGT (iCre-dTAG) MEF cells were plated 24 h before treatment in DMEM + 10% FBS + 1× Pen/Strep. Medium was changed to DMEM + 10% FBS + 1× Pen/Strep + 500 nM dTAG-13 (diluted from 10 mM stock in DMSO) at time zero. Every 24 h, medium was removed and replaced with DMEM + 10% FBS + 1× Pen/Strep with 500 nM dTAG-13 until cell collection.

### Cell Culture and Immunoprecipitation.

iCre-dTAG MEFs expressing the desired ectopic OGT variants were seeded into 15 cm sterile culture dishes at ~13 million cells/dish in DMEM (Thermo Fisher 10567-022) supplemented with 10% FBS and 1× Pen/Strep antibiotics. After 12 h, the medium was replaced with fresh complete DMEM + 500 nM dTAG-13. After 8 h of dTAG- 13 treatment, cells were harvested by scraping in cold PBS and pelleted at 500 × g, 4 °C, for 5 min. Pellets were lysed on ice with homemade Pierce IP Lysis Buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl pH = 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1% IGEPAL CA-630, and 5% glycerol) supplemented with 1× Halt Protease and Phosphatase Inhibitor Cocktail (Thermo Scientific, 78440). Lysates were spun in a tabletop centrifuge at max speed for 10 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was transferred to a chilled tube, and a BCA assay was performed to determine the total protein concentration. 55 μL of packed anti-FLAG M2 magnetic beads (Millipore Sigma M8823-5ML) were washed 3× with 300 μL cold Tris-buffered saline (TBS), then were loaded with 440 μL of lysate (2,400 μg total protein). Samples were incubated overnight at 4 °C, rotating end-over-end to enable protein binding to the beads. After 11 h of incubation, the flowthrough was collected, and beads were washed 2× with 400 μL of cold TBS, rotating for 5 min at 4 °C. Beads were then washed 2× with 400 μL of cold HEPES-buffered saline (HBS), rotating for 5 min at 4 °C. Then, 200 μL of 5% formic acid (Thermo Fisher 28905) was added to the beads, and they were rotated for 20 min at room temperature. The elution was collected and then repeated with another 200 μL of fresh 5% formic acid. Both elutions were combined for a total of 400 μL of eluted protein in 5% formic acid.

### Protein Digestion and Preparation for Mass Spectrometry Analysis.

The elution samples were dried by vacuum centrifugation. The samples were then resuspended in 100 μL of 100 mM HEPES, pH 8.5, and digested at 37 °C with trypsin at a 100:1 protein-to-protease ratio overnight. The samples were desalted via StageTip, dried via vacuum centrifugation, and reconstituted in 5% acetonitrile and 5% formic acid for Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry/mass spectrometry (LCMS/MS) processing.

### Mass Spectrometric Data Collection.

Mass spectrometry data were collected using an Exploris 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled with a Proxeon 1200 Liquid Chromatograph (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were separated on a 100 μm inner diameter microcapillary column packed with ~25 cm of Accucore C18 resin (2.6 μm, 150 Å, Thermo Fisher Scientific). ~1 μg was loaded onto the column. Peptides were separated using a 90min gradient of 3 to 25% acetonitrile in 0.125% formic acid with a flow rate of 520 nL/min. The scan sequence began with an Orbitrap MS1 spectrum with the following parameters: resolution 60,000, scan range 350 to 1,350 Th, automatic gain control (AGC) target “standard”, maximum injection time “auto”, radiofrequency (RF) lens setting 40%, and centroid spectrum data type. We selected the top twenty precursors for MS2 analysis which consisted of high-energy collision dissociation (HCD) with the following parameters: resolution 15,000, AGC was set at standard, maximum injection time auto, isolation window 0.7 Th, normalized collision energy 28, and centroid spectrum data type. In addition, unassigned and singly charged species were excluded from MS2 analysis, and dynamic exclusion was set to 90 s.
